cells.tense: Right here at the table, the pen moving and the whole shape already in view.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling
cells.ask: Take one old hurt you keep going back over. Say what's actually fair — what it cost, what it deserves — and then let the matter close. No second hearing.
cells.core:
You can see the whole of something from just outside it and still be standing in the middle of it. When a thing among your people has run its course, you know, and you let it finish without needing anyone to agree first — and afterwards the room is quieter than anyone expected. The ends you make don't land like losses on the ones nearby. Nobody has to justify themselves before you'll let them be done.

One feeling is still open in your hand past its finish. Name what's fair in it, for them and for you, and be done with it the same day. It needs no company and no reason given. What you get is the cleared ground, which is what you've been circling anyway. If somebody notices you seem lighter and asks why, you can honestly say you don't know.

cells.tense: Soon, braced for something that hasn't happened, pen hovering above a page that isn't written yet.
cells.act: ask how it feels to them and stay with the answer
cells.ask: Next time someone close brings you something heavy, ask how it feels from where they're sitting, then stay quiet for a minute after they answer. Don't sort it for them.
cells.core:
You catch the shape of a thing early, and lately you've been handing people that shape before they've had their own time inside it. You name the ending for them, point toward the next stretch, and the caring underneath is genuine — it just arrives before they've finished standing where they are. From their side, something closes before they've said a word about it. Tidy, and not finished.

Let catching it wait one conversation. Ask what it's like from inside, then hold still while they tell you — don't hand them the pattern, don't say what it means. You'll come away knowing something you didn't. It'll be theirs, and you'll have been there when it arrived, which is the part that holds.

cells.tense: At a door that's already behind you, your hand still holding the pen from last year.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Give ten minutes this week to something you'd choose anyway — not a plan, not a promise. Stop before it turns into one. The next ten can wait until the first exists.
cells.core:
Something finished a while back, and part of you hasn't left the doorway of it. The pattern you used to take in whole has narrowed — you catch what's failing, not what's forming, and the next thing hasn't been picked up because the last one hasn't been put down. It isn't that you've gone cold. You're in the frame, coat on, no address yet. The ones who lean on the floor you keep can feel your hand isn't in it.

Give ten minutes to a small want this week. Not a goal, not a commitment — ten minutes on something you'd pick anyway, then close it before it becomes a plan. What you're looking for won't announce itself. It shows up somewhere in the middle of the ten minutes, and then again next week. Keep it that small.

cells.tense: With the pen down, your hand still tracing the page you're already writing.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Plenty of advice you've given others, you haven't taken yourself. Do one piece of the thing you keep circling today, and don't announce it first. One move, and it's already different.
cells.core:
People bring you the tangle, you spread it out where it can be seen, and they walk off holding the shape and calling it their own working-out. The organizing is your hand. You've been filing it under how things happen to sort themselves out. The ones who use the flat surface can't tell who laid it down.

Standing still isn't a mood for you; it's a decision you haven't made yet. Do the smallest piece of whatever you keep circling — today, no build-up, no announcement. You won't feel like it beforehand, and you don't need to. Notice that the air moves after. That was your hand, and now it's on record, for them and for you.
